module_title: Introduction to Pig Nutrition and Feed Formulation

lessons.title: Overview of Pig Production Systems and Feeding Stages
lessons.body: Pig production in Africa ranges from backyard scavenging to intensive commercial units. In backyard systems, pigs eat household waste, roots, and whatever they find, often resulting in slow growth (6-12 months to reach 80 kg). In semi-intensive systems, farmers provide some feed (e.g., 1-2 kg of maize bran per day) and let pigs forage. Intensive systems confine pigs and rely entirely on formulated feed, aiming for 100 kg in 5-6 months. Feeding stages depend on age and weight: creep feed for piglets (0-4 weeks, 20% protein), starter (4-10 weeks, 18% protein), grower (10-20 weeks, 16% protein), and finisher (20-28 weeks, 14% protein). Sows and boars have special diets: gestation (12-14% protein), lactation (16-18% protein). In Africa, many farmers mix their own feed using locally available ingredients like maize, cassava, soybean meal, and fish meal. However, without proper formulation, pigs may suffer from nutrient deficiencies, leading to poor growth and disease. For example, a 50 kg grower pig needs about 1.8 kg of feed per day (dry matter basis) containing 16% crude protein, 0.6% calcium, and 0.5% phosphorus. Water is critical: a pig drinks 2-3 times its feed intake. In hot climates, water intake can double. Understanding these stages helps you adjust feed to match the pig's changing needs, saving money and maximizing growth. Always weigh pigs monthly to track progress and adjust feed amounts. Use a simple scale or weigh tape to estimate weight.

lessons.title: Basic Nutrient Requirements of Pigs: Water, Energy, Protein, Minerals, Vitamins
lessons.body: Pigs need six nutrient groups: water, energy, protein, minerals, vitamins, and sometimes additives. Water is the most critical: a 50 kg pig drinks 5-10 litres daily; a lactating sow can drink 20-30 litres. Lack of water reduces feed intake and growth. Energy comes mainly from carbohydrates (maize, cassava, sorghum) and fats/oils. Pigs need energy for maintenance and growth. A grower pig requires about 13-14 MJ digestible energy per kg feed. In Africa, maize is the top energy source, but cassava can replace up to 50% if balanced with protein. Protein is needed for muscle and tissue. Crude protein (CP) requirements: piglets 20-22%, growers 16-18%, finishers 14-16%, gestating sows 12-14%, lactating sows 16-18%. Protein is made of amino acids; lysine is the most limiting. A grower diet should have 0.8-0.9% lysine. Sources include soybean meal (44-48% CP), fish meal (60-65% CP), and groundnut cake (40-45% CP). Minerals: calcium and phosphorus are key for bones. A grower diet needs 0.6-0.8% calcium and 0.5-0.6% phosphorus, with a calcium-to-phosphorus ratio of 1.2:1 to 1.5:1. Salt (0.2-0.3%) provides sodium and chloride. Vitamins: pigs need vitamins A, D, E, K, and B-complex. Under African conditions, green forage like sweet potato vines or amaranth can supply some vitamins, but commercial premixes are safer. For example, add 0.25% vitamin-mineral premix to the diet. Always provide clean water and a balanced diet to avoid deficiencies like rickets (from lack of calcium/phosphorus) or poor growth (from lack of lysine).

lessons.title: Digestive Anatomy and Physiology of Pigs
lessons.body: Pigs are monogastric (single-stomach) animals, meaning they cannot digest large amounts of fibre like ruminants. Their digestive system includes the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine. Digestion starts in the mouth: pigs chew feed and mix it with saliva containing amylase, which begins starch breakdown. The stomach is a simple, single-chamber organ that secretes hydrochloric acid and pepsin to digest proteins. The stomach has a capacity of about 2-3 litres in a 50 kg pig. From the stomach, feed enters the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), where most digestion and absorption occur. The pancreas and liver release enzymes (trypsin, chymotrypsin, lipase) and bile to break down proteins, fats, and carbohydrates. The small intestine is about 15-20 metres long in adult pigs. Nutrients are absorbed through villi. The large intestine (caecum and colon) ferments some fibre and absorbs water and minerals. Pigs have a functional caecum but it is less developed than in horses. Fibre digestion is limited; therefore, high-fibre feeds like grass or straw should be restricted. For example, a diet with more than 10% crude fibre reduces feed intake and growth. In Africa, farmers often use fibrous by-products like maize cobs or rice bran; these should be limited to 5-10% of the diet. Understanding digestion helps you choose ingredients that pigs can actually use. For instance, finely ground maize is better digested than whole kernels. Also, pigs need constant access to water because digestion requires moisture. A pig's digestive tract is adapted to a omnivorous diet, so both plant and animal proteins can be used, but plant sources like soybean meal must be processed (heated) to destroy anti-nutritional factors like trypsin inhibitors.

lessons.title: Feed Ingredients Classification and Terminology
lessons.body: Feed ingredients are classified into eight groups by the Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO): dry forages and roughages, pasture, silage, energy feeds, protein supplements, mineral supplements, vitamin supplements, and additives. In Africa, common energy feeds include maize (8-9% CP, 3.3-3.5 Mcal/kg DE), cassava (2-3% CP, high starch), sorghum, and wheat bran. Protein supplements: soybean meal (44-48% CP), groundnut cake (40-45% CP), fish meal (60-65% CP), and cottonseed cake (30-35% CP, but limited by gossypol). Mineral supplements: limestone (calcium), dicalcium phosphate (calcium and phosphorus), and salt. Vitamin supplements: commercial premixes. Additives: antibiotics (for disease control, but use with caution), enzymes (phytase to improve phosphorus digestibility), and antioxidants. Terminology: 'as-fed' means feed as it is offered, including moisture; 'dry matter' (DM) is feed minus moisture. For example, maize at 12% moisture has 88% DM. 'Crude protein' (CP) is nitrogen content multiplied by 6.25. 'Digestible energy' (DE) is the energy available to the pig after digestion. 'Metabolizable energy' (ME) is DE minus energy lost in urine and gases. In feed formulation, you balance nutrients on a DM basis. For instance, a grower diet might be 88% DM, 16% CP, 0.7% calcium, 0.6% phosphorus. Locally available ingredients like palm kernel cake (15-18% CP) can be used but are high in fibre. Always test ingredients for quality: mouldy maize can contain aflatoxins, which are poisonous to pigs. Store feed in dry, cool places. Use a hammer mill to grind ingredients to the right particle size (500-800 microns for maize) to improve digestion. Mixing by hand or with a small mixer should be thorough to avoid segregation.

lessons.title: Role of a Feed Formulator in Pig Production
lessons.body: A feed formulator is the person who designs diets that meet the nutrient needs of pigs at the lowest cost. In Africa, this role is often taken by the farmer or a hired nutritionist. The formulator must know the nutrient requirements of different pig classes (e.g., grower, finisher, sow) and the nutrient composition of available ingredients. They use tools like the Pearson Square method for simple two-ingredient mixes, or computer software (e.g., WinFeed, Feedsoft) for complex formulations. The formulator's main tasks: (1) Determine the nutrient requirements based on pig weight, age, and production stage. (2) Select locally available and cost-effective ingredients. (3) Calculate the proportions of each ingredient to meet requirements. (4) Check that the final mix meets minimum and maximum limits for nutrients and anti-nutritional factors. (5) Ensure the feed is palatable and safe. For example, a formulator might use the Pearson Square to mix maize (8.5% CP) and soybean meal (44% CP) to make a 16% CP grower diet. The formula: parts of maize = (44-16) = 28; parts of soybean meal = (16-8.5) = 7.5; total parts = 35.5. So maize = 28/35.5 = 78.9%, soybean meal = 7.5/35.5 = 21.1%. Then add minerals and vitamins. The formulator also monitors feed costs: in many African countries, feed accounts for 60-70% of pig production costs. By using alternative ingredients like cassava or palm kernel cake, they can reduce costs. However, they must balance amino acids, especially lysine, methionine, and tryptophan. A good formulator keeps records of pig performance and adjusts formulas as needed. They also train farm workers on proper mixing and feeding. Without a skilled formulator, pigs may get too much or too little of certain nutrients, leading to poor growth, disease, or wasted money.

lessons.title: Current Trends and Challenges in Pig Feed Formulation
lessons.body: In Africa, pig feed formulation faces both opportunities and challenges. Trends: (1) Use of alternative feed ingredients: cassava, sweet potato, palm kernel cake, and brewery waste are increasingly used to reduce reliance on expensive maize and soybean meal. For example, cassava can replace up to 50% of maize in grower diets if supplemented with methionine and lysine. (2) Precision feeding: using phase feeding (adjusting diets as pigs grow) to match nutrients exactly, reducing waste. (3) Use of enzymes: phytase to release phosphorus from plant sources, reducing need for expensive dicalcium phosphate. (4) Antibiotic-free feeds: due to rising antimicrobial resistance, farmers use probiotics, prebiotics, and organic acids. (5) Digital tools: mobile apps like Feed Formulation for Pigs help farmers calculate rations. Challenges: (1) High cost and inconsistent supply of quality ingredients. Maize prices fluctuate, and aflatoxin contamination is common. (2) Lack of accurate nutrient composition data for local ingredients. For instance, the protein content of groundnut cake can vary from 30% to 50%. (3) Limited access to laboratory analysis. (4) Poor storage leading to mould and insect damage. (5) Inadequate training: many farmers mix feed by guesswork, leading to imbalances. (6) Climate change affecting crop yields. To overcome these, formulators should: test ingredients regularly, use least-cost formulation software, join cooperatives to buy ingredients in bulk, and attend training. For example, in Kenya, farmers use a simple spreadsheet to formulate rations based on local prices. In Nigeria, the use of cassava peel meal in pig diets has been researched. By staying updated, you can produce affordable, nutritious feed that boosts pig production and profits. Remember, a well-formulated feed can improve feed conversion ratio from 4:1 to 3:1, saving 25% on feed costs.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Pig Feed Formulation in African Agribusiness

Feed represents 65â75% of the total cost of pig production in most African systems. For a commercial piggery in Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda, or South Africa, every 1% reduction in feed cost per kilogram of gain translates directly into margin. This practical reference distils the essentials of pig nutrition and feed formulation into an operational guide for farm managers, feed millers, and agripreneurs who need to make decisions â not just understand theory.

Whether you are formulating for a 50-sow unit in Kiambu County or a 5,000-pig integrator in Ogun State, the principles are the same: match nutrients to the pig's stage of production, source ingredients locally and competitively, and control the factors that erode feed value â moisture, mycotoxins, anti-nutritional factors, and mixing errors.

Why Digestive Anatomy Drives Formulation Decisions

The pig is a monogastric (single-stomach) omnivore. Unlike ruminants, it cannot efficiently ferment fibrous feeds â so high-fibre ingredients like maize bran, rice bran, and palm kernel cake must be limited. The stomach's low pH (1.5â3.5) activates pepsin for protein digestion; the small intestine absorbs amino acids, simple sugars, and fatty acids; the large intestine ferments some fibre and absorbs water and minerals. This anatomy explains why weaner pigs (7â15 kg) need highly digestible, low-fibre diets with milk proteins and cooked cereals, while finishers can utilise more by-products.

In African contexts, this is a business constraint: cheap fibrous by-products that work for cattle will depress pig growth and feed conversion ratio (FCR). The formulator's job is to find the sweet spot â maximum inclusion of local by-products without sacrificing performance.

Nutrient Requirement Priorities by Stage

Water is the most critical nutrient â pigs consume 2â3 litres per kg of dry feed, and lactating sows up to 30â40 litres per day. Water restriction is the fastest way to kill performance. Energy (from maize, cassava, sorghum, wheat) drives growth; protein (from soybean meal, sunflower cake, fishmeal, cottonseed cake) supplies amino acids â lysine, methionine, threonine, and tryptophan are usually first-limiting. Minerals (calcium, phosphorus, zinc, iron, selenium) and vitamins (A, D, E, K, B-complex) are needed in small but non-negotiable quantities.

Feed Ingredient Classification â The African Context

Ingredients fall into five classes: energy sources (maize, cassava chips, sorghum, wheat bran), protein sources (soybean meal, sunflower cake, fishmeal, cottonseed cake, groundnut cake), mineral sources (limestone, dicalcium phosphate, bone meal, oyster shell), vitamin sources (premixes), and additives (amino acids, enzymes, probiotics, mycotoxin binders). In Africa, availability and price volatility dictate formulation. Maize competes with human food; cassava and sorghum become attractive substitutes when processed correctly. Soybean meal is often imported and expensive â sunflower cake, cottonseed cake, and locally produced fishmeal offer alternatives, provided anti-nutritional factors (gossypol in cottonseed, trypsin inhibitors in raw soy) are managed.

Role of the Feed Formulator

The formulator sits at the intersection of nutrition science, procurement, and finance. Core responsibilities: (1) define nutrient specifications by stage; (2) select ingredients based on cost per unit of nutrient, not cost per tonne; (3) balance amino acids, energy, minerals, and vitamins using linear programming or least-cost software; (4) verify ingredient quality on arrival (moisture, protein, mycotoxins); (5) monitor FCR, average daily gain (ADG), and cost per kg gain; (6) adjust formulations as ingredient prices shift. In African agribusiness, the formulator often doubles as procurement officer and quality controller â making discipline and record-keeping as important as nutritional knowledge.

Current Trends and Challenges

Trends: rising demand for pork in Africa (FAO projects strong growth in West and East Africa); adoption of Least-Cost Feed Formulation software; use of exogenous enzymes (phytase, xylanase) to unlock nutrients from cheaper ingredients; precision feeding and phase feeding; growth of commercial feed mills and contract farming.

Challenges: volatile maize and soybean prices; aflatoxin and fumonisin contamination in maize and groundnut cake; foreign exchange constraints on imported premixes and amino acids; inconsistent ingredient quality; limited laboratory testing capacity; competition with human food for maize and soy; and climate-driven supply shocks.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Mycotoxins and Anti-Nutritional Factors

Never feed mouldy maize, groundnut cake, or cottonseed cake to pigs. Aflatoxin B1 is carcinogenic and causes liver damage, reduced growth, and immunosuppression; even low levels (20â50 ppb) depress performance. Fumonisins cause pulmonary oedema in pigs. Gossypol in cottonseed cake causes infertility and heart damage â limit to 10% and only use for finishers, never for breeding stock. Raw soybeans contain trypsin inhibitors that must be destroyed by proper heat treatment (toasting, extrusion). Always test incoming ingredients or use a reputable mycotoxin binder. Store feed below 12% moisture in dry, ventilated conditions. Suspect contamination is a business risk â one bad batch can wipe out a herd's productivity and your reputation.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Know your stage: Confirm the correct nutrient specification for creep, starter, grower, finisher, or sow â do not use one diet across all stages.
  • Water first: Verify clean, unlimited water supply (2â3 L/kg feed; 30â40 L/day for lactating sows) before anything else.
  • Cost per nutrient: Compare ingredients on cost per kg of digestible lysine and ME, not cost per tonne.
  • Test every batch: Check moisture (<12%), crude protein, and mycotoxins on arrival â reject suspect loads.
  • Respect inclusion limits: Cap fibrous by-products, cottonseed cake, and cassava according to stage-specific maxima.
  • Balance amino acids: Use synthetic lysine, methionine, and threonine to reduce crude protein and cost while maintaining performance.
  • Monitor performance: Track FCR, ADG, and cost per kg gain weekly; adjust formulation when prices or performance shift.
  • Store correctly: Keep feed dry, cool, ventilated, and off the floor; use within 4â6 weeks to prevent mould and rancidity.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Pig Sector Manual: Good Practices for the Pig Meat Sector (FAO, 2012) â free download, covers nutrition, feeding, and African production systems.
  • Feedipedia â Animal Feed Resources Information System (INRAE, CIRAD, AFZ, FAO) â free database of ingredient composition and anti-nutritional factors.
  • NRC (2012) Nutrient Requirements of Swine, 11th Revised Edition â National Academies Press; free read online, authoritative nutrient specifications.
  • International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) â free publications on smallholder pig systems and feed resources in Africa.
  • World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) â free standards on animal feed safety and antimicrobial use in pig production.

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course Pig Feed Formulation. Practical Reference content is intended for training and operational decision support; always verify ingredient composition locally and consult a qualified nutritionist before finalising commercial formulations.

quiz.q: What is the typical crude protein requirement for a grower pig (10-20 weeks old)?
quiz.explanation: Grower pigs need 16-18% crude protein for optimal muscle growth.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is most critical for pigs and often overlooked?
quiz.explanation: Water is essential for all body functions and pigs can die faster from lack of water than food.

quiz.q: In pig digestion, where does most nutrient absorption occur?
quiz.explanation: The small intestine has villi that absorb most nutrients from digested feed.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common energy feed used in African pig diets?
quiz.explanation: Maize is a primary energy source, rich in starch and digestible energy.

quiz.q: What is the main role of a feed formulator?
options: A) To feed the pigs daily
B) To design least-cost diets meeting nutrient requirements
C) To clean the pig pens
quiz.explanation: A feed formulator creates balanced rations that meet nutritional needs at the lowest cost.

quiz.q: Which amino acid is most limiting in typical pig diets based on maize and soybean meal?
quiz.explanation: Lysine is the first limiting amino acid in most cereal-based pig diets.

quiz.q: What is the recommended calcium to phosphorus ratio in pig diets?
quiz.explanation: A ratio of 1.2:1 to 1.5:1 calcium to phosphorus is ideal for bone development.

quiz.q: Which feed ingredient is a good source of protein but must be heated to destroy trypsin inhibitors?
quiz.explanation: Raw soybean meal contains trypsin inhibitors that reduce protein digestion; heating destroys them.

quiz.q: In the Pearson Square method, if you mix maize (8.5% CP) and soybean meal (44% CP) to get 16% CP, what percentage of soybean meal is needed?
quiz.explanation: Using Pearson Square: parts soybean meal = (16-8.5)=7.5; total parts=35.5; 7.5/35.5=21.1%.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a current trend in pig feed formulation in Africa?
options: B) Use of alternative ingredients like cassava
quiz.explanation: Farmers are using cassava and other local ingredients to reduce feed costs.

quiz.q: What is the typical daily water intake for a 50 kg grower pig?
quiz.explanation: A 50 kg pig drinks about 5-10 litres daily, depending on climate and feed.

quiz.q: Which vitamin deficiency can cause rickets in pigs?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin D is needed for calcium and phosphorus absorption; deficiency leads to rickets.

quiz.q: What is the main function of the stomach in pig digestion?
quiz.explanation: The stomach secretes acid and pepsin to begin protein digestion.

quiz.q: Which feed ingredient is classified as a protein supplement?
quiz.explanation: Fish meal is high in protein (60-65% CP) and is a protein supplement.

quiz.q: What does 'as-fed' basis mean in feed formulation?
options: B) Feed as it is offered, including moisture
quiz.explanation: As-fed refers to the feed in its natural state, including its moisture content.

quiz.q: Which of these is a challenge in pig feed formulation in Africa?
options: A) Abundant supply of quality ingredients
B) Lack of accurate nutrient composition data
quiz.explanation: Nutrient composition of local ingredients varies, making formulation difficult.

quiz.q: What is the recommended inclusion rate of salt in pig diets?
quiz.explanation: Salt provides sodium and chloride; 0.2-0.3% is typical.

quiz.q: Which enzyme is commonly added to pig feed to improve phosphorus digestibility?
quiz.explanation: Phytase breaks down phytate, releasing phosphorus for absorption.

quiz.q: What is the typical feed conversion ratio (FCR) for a well-fed pig?
quiz.explanation: A good FCR is around 3:1 to 4:1 kg feed per kg gain.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of aflatoxin poisoning in pigs?
options: B) Reduced feed intake and liver damage
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxins cause reduced feed intake, liver damage, and poor growth.

quiz.q: What is the main energy unit used in pig feed formulation?
quiz.explanation: Digestible energy is the energy available to the pig after digestion.

quiz.q: Which stage of pig production requires the highest protein percentage?
quiz.explanation: Piglet starter diets need 20-22% CP for rapid growth.

quiz.q: What is the role of the large intestine in pig digestion?
options: B) Ferment fibre and absorb water
quiz.explanation: The large intestine ferments some fibre and absorbs water and minerals.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common mineral supplement in pig diets?
quiz.explanation: Limestone is a source of calcium for bone development.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended inclusion of crude fibre in pig diets?
quiz.explanation: High fibre (>10%) reduces feed intake and nutrient digestibility.

quiz.q: Which of these tools can help a feed formulator balance rations?
quiz.explanation: The Pearson Square is a simple manual method for balancing two ingredients.

quiz.q: What is the typical protein content of fish meal?
quiz.explanation: Fish meal is a high-quality protein source with 60-65% crude protein.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good source of vitamins for pigs in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Green forages like sweet potato vines provide vitamins A and E.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of precision feeding?
options: A) To feed all pigs the same diet
B) To match nutrients exactly to pig needs
quiz.explanation: Precision feeding tailors diets to specific stages, reducing waste and cost.

quiz.q: Which of these is a digital tool for feed formulation?
quiz.explanation: WinFeed is a computer software used for least-cost feed formulation.
